theater: 蜀道北段利州白水江谷地

battle.name: 利州之戰
battle.theater: 蜀道北段利州白水江谷地
battle.brief: 太建十一年（580）秋，陳朝趁北周主力南調豫東攻睢陽，遣蜀軍自閬中、昭化北上，進攻蜀道北門利州（治今廣元）。北周守軍據城死守，城頭弩砲與連發弩壓制攻城步卒，陳軍攻之不克而退。卡面秦連弩屬弩機源流，與本役現場的漢弩一系連弩不同形制，並非現場實物。

kit.name: 秦連弩
kit.history: 弩機把拉力存起來，一踩一發。守城的一方靠它把攻城的人壓在牆外。

countries: 這場戰爭是南朝陳朝與北周在蜀道北段的一場邊境交鋒，時間在公元580年，即陳宣帝太建十一年、北周靜帝宇文闡在位而大冢宰宇文護專政的年份。陳朝一方以益州為大本營，從成都平原各郡徵發州兵與郡兵，由益州刺史、都督一級的將領節制，沿蜀道北段北進；蜀境內設劍門、昭化、白水等關戍，利州（治今四川廣元）一線原由北周控制，陳軍此役的目的，正是在北周主力南調之際奪取這座蜀道北門，進而圖謀漢中與隴右方向。北周一方則以益州為後方，以梁州、興州（漢中）一線的守軍為前沿，兵員多由關中、隴右調發與蜀地徵發混編，騎兵比重明顯高於陳軍，統屬益州總管節制。北周大軍主力由宇文護調派，楊堅隨軍專責東路即豫東睢陽的戰事，蜀北一線的處置權落在益州方面的將領手上，雙方在同一時段內各守一端、互不相援。陳朝一方的指揮鏈條較長，蜀境調兵須有詔檄往還，宣帝晚年多臥病，政令多出中書監、吏部尚書一班文臣之手，邊事的決策與出兵往往相隔數月。北周方面則在宇文氏宗室、宇文護與楊堅三方角力之下運作，前線將領既要應付蜀北的牽制，又要在關中宿衛與南征之間抽調兵源，蜀道上的兵力和糧秣補充因此格外吃力。
countriesEn: This war was a frontier clash on the northern stretch of the Shu road between the Southern Chen court and the Zhou dynasty of the North, fought in 580 CE, the eleventh year of the Taijian era under Emperor Xuan of Chen, at a time when the young Emperor Jing of Zhou, Yuwen Chan, sat on the throne while the grand chancellor Yuwen Hu held the real power. On the Chen side the base of operations was Yizhou: troops were levied from the commanderies of the Chengdu plain, both provincial and district soldiers, and placed under a commander of the rank of inspector of Yizhou or military governor, and they moved north along the northern Shu road. Inside its own borders Chen had established the passes of Jianmen, Zhaohua and Baishui, while the line of Lizhou, at present-day Guangyuan in Sichuan, had been held by the Zhou. The object of the Chen offensive in this campaign was precisely to seize that northern gate of the Shu road while the Zhou main force was drawn away southward, and from there to aim at Hanzhong and the Longyou direction. The Zhou side used Yizhou as its rear, with the garrisons of Liangzhou and Xingzhou, that is Hanzhong, forming its forward line; its soldiers were a mixture of units transferred from Guanzhong and Longyou with men levied in Shu itself, and the proportion of cavalry in its ranks was markedly higher than in the Chen army, all under the inspector-general of Yizhou. The Zhou main army was dispatched by Yuwen Hu, while Yang Jian accompanied it and took charge of the eastern theatre, the campaign against Suiyang in eastern Henan. The conduct of the fighting along the northern Shu road fell to the commanders on the Yizhou side, so that the two sides were each holding one end of the same front and could not assist one another. The Chen command chain was the longer of the two: moving troops in the Shu borderlands required imperial rescripts to travel back and forth, and the aged Xuan emperor spent much of this time in bed, with policy shaped by a group of civil officials such as the director of the secretariat and the minister of the personnel, so that decisions on the frontier and the dispatch of troops were often months apart. The Zhou state, by contrast, operated under a three-way struggle between the Yuwen clan, Yuwen Hu and Yang Jian, and its frontline commanders had to meet the Shu distraction while also drawing men away from the Guanzhong imperial guard for the southern campaign, which made the supply of troops and provisions along the Shu road exceptionally burdensome.
people: 陳宣帝陳頊是這場衝突背後最關鍵的人物。他在即位之前已作為梁朝將領在荊西與北朝周旋十餘年，主政之後又面對一個南北對峙而北強南弱的局面。太建十一年時他年近六十且久病臥床，蜀北的戰事正是在他不能親自處置國事、只能靠一紙詔書遙控的狀況下發動。太子陳伯宗已被立為儲君，此時已成年，卻因性資柔弱而未受重用於軍政；陳後主陳叔寶當時仍以會稽王的身分在東南活動，尚未即位，日後正是由他接手這副因戰敗而更加空虛的江山。陳朝在蜀北的將領姓名沒有留下可靠記載，僅知調度出自益州方面，屬於各郡兵員的臨時集結，而非宿將常備之師。與蜀北戰事同一時段，陳朝最能戰的名將蕭摩訶被放在豫東睢陽方向，率主力抵擋北周南下的重兵；陳朝等於把兩副主力同時投入兩條戰線，任何一線失手都會牽動另一線。北周一邊，靜帝宇文闡年幼，國政盡歸大冢宰宇文護，真正決定戰略取向的是隨國公楊堅，他隨軍南征並直接主持東路，雖不在蜀北現身，但他的態度決定北周可以放手用兵而不必顧忌朝局。蜀地方面，日後在隋朝開皇年間相繼出任益州總管、整頓蜀北防務的韋世康、韋沖等人，其經營的正是這場戰爭留下的邊界線；他們到任後修葺城壘、招撫諸州、恢復驛傳，等於替北周一方收拾了這場交鋒留下的殘局。
peopleEn: Emperor Xuan of Chen, Chen Xu, was the man behind the conflict. Before his accession he had spent more than a decade as a general of the Liang court operating in western Jing against the northern dynasties, and once on the throne he faced a situation in which the north outweighed the south in a rivalry of a century's standing. In the eleventh year of Taijian he was close to sixty and had been bedridden for some time, and the fighting on the northern Shu road was set in motion precisely while he could no longer personally conduct the business of state and could only guide it by rescript from afar. The crown prince Chen Bozong had already been established as heir and was by then an adult, but owing to his soft character he was not entrusted with military or political command; Chen Shubao, the man who would rule as the last emperor of Chen, was still active in the southeast as Prince of Kuaiji and had not yet taken the throne, and it was he who would later inherit an empire emptied further by defeat. No reliable record of the names of the Chen commanders in the north of Shu survives; all that is known is that the deployment came out of Yizhou and amounted to a hastily mustered body of district levies rather than a standing army of seasoned generals. At the same time as the fighting in northern Shu, the ablest commander of the Chen state, Xiao Mohe, was stationed in the Suiyang direction in eastern Henan with the main body of the army to hold off the Zhou forces advancing from the north; the Chen court was thus committing two separate main forces to two fronts at once, and a failure on either front would tell directly on the other. On the Zhou side the child emperor Yuwen Chan could not rule, and all power lay with the grand chancellor Yuwen Hu; the man who really set the strategic direction was Yang Jian, then Duke of Sui, who went with the southern army and personally directed the eastern theatre. Although he did not appear in the north of Shu, his attitude was what allowed the Zhou to fight freely there without fear of the court. As for Shu itself, the men who would in the Kaihuang era of the Sui successively hold the office of inspector-general of Yizhou and rebuild the northern Shu defences, such as Wei Shikang and Wei Chong, took over precisely the boundary line this war had left behind; once in office they repaired the walls, courted the outlying prefectures and restored the post roads, in effect tidying up the aftermath of the clash for the losing side.
kits: 卡面這件秦連弩在戰役中的位置，是在城頭而不是在陣前。弩機把拉力儲存起來，射手踩動踏板即可連續發射，不必反覆上弦，這正是守城一方最需要的東西。牌面所繪屬秦代弩機傳統的源流標本，年份定在公元前二百年上下，與本役現場的形制並不相同：公元五百八十年的蜀道上不可能出現秦弩原物，現場實際使用的是漢弩一系的連發弩（曹魏馬鈞改進之制見於三國志，六世紀時蜀地器型已多失傳），以及把弩機固定在木架上、置於城頭的弩砲，另有弓、投石機、檑木撞車與女牆上應急的礫石火罐。守軍的裝備以弩砲與連發弩為核心，覆蓋城門、塹壕與通往城牆的坡道；步卒披甲執盾，操長戟與環首刀，專司封堵缺口與清剿攀城者，騎兵則在城外出擊，攔截糧道與退兵之路。進攻一方的器械明顯吃虧：雲梯、撞車、蒙衝這類攻城器具在關中與中原容易製造，蜀道運載卻極為吃力，牛皮、巨木與長杆一旦遇上棧道與山口的轉折便難以通過；陳軍多靠步行與肩扛把器械分件運上來，臨時拼裝使用，攻城的連續性與強度都受限。步卒的防護同樣簡陋，陳軍的甲胄以皮甲與札甲為主，兵員大量來自益州各郡的徵發，訓練與裝備不齊。糧秣方面，棧道只容單列縱隊通行，牛馬改為馱運、其餘靠人背肩扛，糧食從成都送到劍門便已耗去大半人力；反觀守方，由關中與隴右運來的物資要經劍閣道與金牛道入蜀，距離更遠，同樣吃力。
kitsEn: The place of the repeating crossbow on this card is on the wall, not in the line of battle. The trigger mechanism stores the pull of the bow, and the shooter looses a bolt by pressing a tread, without having to draw and reload the bow for every shot, and that is exactly what a defending garrison most needed. What the card depicts is a specimen of the Qin tradition of crossbow mechanism, dated to around 200 BC, and it is not the same form as anything on the field in this campaign: no actual Qin crossbow could have stood on a Shu road in 580 CE. What was used on the spot was the repeating crossbow of the Han line, of which the version improved by Ma Jun of Cao Wei is described in the Records of the Three Kingdoms and of which the local forms had largely been lost by the sixth century, together with the crossbow bolt shooter, a mechanism fixed on a timber frame and set on the wall, and besides these a bow, a traction trebuchet, a battering ram and the stones and fire pots kept ready on the parapet for emergencies. The garrison was organised around the bolt shooters and the repeating crossbows, whose arcs covered the gate, the ditch and the slope leading up to the curtain wall; the foot soldiers were armoured and carried shields, pikes and ring-pommel sabres, and their task was to plug breaches and to cut up those who had scaled the wall, while the cavalry operated outside the walls to intercept the supply line and the roads of retreat. The attacking side was clearly at a disadvantage in siege equipment: ladders, rams and the hide-covered assault carts were easy to build in Guanzhong and the Central Plain, but almost impossible to carry along the Shu road, since hides, heavy timber and long poles could not negotiate the cliff galleries and the sharp turns at the passes. The Chen troops had the bulk of their equipment carried up in pieces on foot and assembled on the spot, which limited both the continuity and the weight of their assaults. Their protection was poor as well: the Chen armour was largely leather and small-plate, the soldiers were for the most part levies from the commanderies of Yizhou, and they were neither well trained nor well equipped. Supply was just as bad on the attacker side. The cliff galleries took a single file abreast, so pack animals were used for the loads and the remainder carried on the backs of men; by the time grain had been brought from Chengdu to Jianmen most of the human effort was already spent. The defenders had no advantage either: supplies from Guanzhong and Longyou had to come into Shu by the Jiange road and the Jinniu road, a longer run, and equally hard.
tactics: 蜀道決定了這場戰爭的樣子。從劍門關到利州一線，山路在懸崖與溪谷之間盤旋，寬處不過容得下兩三輛車並排，最窄處只容一列縱隊通過，兩側是難以攀越的峭壁。陳軍的進攻因此只能拉成一條長而單薄的縱隊：先出遊騎遮蔽白水江谷地，步卒沿官道逐段推進，每通過一段棧道才敢展開一次；攻城器械必須拆成部件由人力運上山口再就地拼裝，難以一次投入多具而同時進攻。逼城之後的作戰分三步：先用弩砲與矢石對射，壓制城頭守兵使其不能探身射擊；再把雲梯、撞車、蒙衝推到城下坡地，以盾陣掩護器械緩慢前進；最後才是步卒結隊攀城，每批攻勢都很短，攻城隊伍屢進屢退。守方依山勢分段佈防，弩砲分層架設，射界交錯覆蓋城門前坡與兩側隘口，並派步騎由側門出城切糧與斷退路，糧道被截就等於逼攻方退兵。時間也是攻方的敵人：秋後山雨使棧道泥濘，糧秣車隊遲滯，遠征軍士久役疲敝，攻勢拖得越久越難以為繼。雙方的體系也不相稱，陳側的益州兵需經劍門北運糧，北周側關中援兵卻要經劍閣道入蜀，兩條補給線都極脆弱，戰線拉得越長越難收攏，故此役全程都未曾形成包圍或會師攻擊。
tacticsEn: The Shu road decided the character of this war. From the pass of Jianmen to Lizhou the mountain track wound between cliffs and ravines; at its widest it would take two or three carts abreast, at its narrowest a single file, with rock walls on either side that could not be climbed. The Chen attack could therefore only be drawn out into a long, thin column: cavalry scouts first screened the valley of the Baishui river, the foot soldiers pushed along the road stage by stage, and only dared deploy after each stretch of cliff gallery had been passed. Siege equipment had to be broken down into components, carried up to the pass on men's backs and assembled on the spot, and it was impossible to bring up several machines at once and have them assault together. Once in contact with the walls the assault was carried out in three steps. First the bolt shooters and stone throwers duelled across the wall to pin down the defenders so that they could not lean out to shoot. Then ladders, rams and hide-covered carts were pushed forward on the slope below the walls, screened by shield formations and advanced slowly. Only then did the foot soldiers form up to scale the wall, and each effort was short, the assaulting columns advancing and falling back repeatedly. The defenders disposed their troops in sections according to the lie of the hills, mounted the bolt shooters in tiers, laid their arcs so as to cross-cover the slope in front of the gate and the defiles on either flank, and sent foot and horse out of the side gates to cut the supply line and the roads of retreat; once the grain road was cut the attackers were in effect forced to withdraw. Time was the attacker's enemy as well: after the autumn rains the cliff galleries turned to mud, the supply columns fell behind, a far-marching army wore out with long service, and the longer the assault dragged on the harder it was to sustain. The two systems of supply did not match either. The Chen troops in Yizhou had to move their grain north through Jianmen, while the Zhou reinforcements from Guanzhong had to come into Shu by the Jiange road; both lines of supply were extremely fragile, and the longer the frontage was stretched the harder it was to close it up. For that reason the campaign never at any point produced an envelopment or a joined assault.
data: 可核的數字有限，先說年份：580年，陳太建十一年；翌年隋代周，改元開皇；開皇九年隋滅陳，蜀地盡入一統。距離上，利州治今廣元，至劍門關約一百三十公里，至成都約四百五十公里；白水江谷地通道綿延數十公里，是白水關與蜀北唯一可通車之路。蜀道棧道寬處可容二三輛車並行，窄處僅容一車，兵隊縱隊前後相望而不相及。弩砲是守城主要遠射兵器，有效射程約一百五十至二百米，遠超弓箭，故守方據城即可控制攻城步兵的集結地；連發弩則補足覆蓋城頭與隘口的射界。蜀中郡兵徵發數量與雙方斬獲數字，現存史料未詳載，本紀不作臆補：可確定的是陳軍未攻下城池，且攻勢止步於蜀道北段而未進入益州平原，交戰雙方均未達到殲滅對方一部的規模。利州之名與區劃在隋平陳之後仍沿用，廣元一帶的行政隸屬此後屢經調整，亦可反推此役歸屬。
dataEn: The verifiable figures are few, and the year comes first: 580, the eleventh year of Taijian under Chen; in the following year the Sui replaced the Zhou and opened the Kaihuang era; in the ninth year of Kaihuang the Sui destroyed Chen and Shu was gathered into a single administration. As for distances, Lizhou was at present-day Guangyuan, about one hundred and thirty kilometres from the pass of Jianmen and about four hundred and fifty kilometres from Chengdu; the road through the valley of the Baishui river ran for several dozen kilometres and was the only wheeled route between the pass of Baishui and the north of Shu. The cliff galleries of the Shu road were wide enough for two or three carts abreast at the best and for a single cart at the worst, so that columns of troops saw one another ahead and behind without ever drawing level. The bolt shooter was the principal long-range arm of the defence, with an effective range of roughly one hundred and fifty to two hundred metres, well beyond that of arrows, so that by holding the city the defenders controlled the ground on which the attacking infantry had to mass; the repeating crossbow then filled out the arcs over the wall and the defiles. The numbers of district levies raised in Shu and the casualty and capture returns of both sides are not recorded in the surviving sources, and this account will not invent them. What can be established is that the Chen army did not take the city, and that its advance stopped on the northern stretch of the Shu road without ever reaching the plain of Yizhou; neither side achieved the destruction of a single enemy formation. The name of Lizhou and its administrative division survived the Sui conquest of Chen, and the subsequent repeated readjustment of the jurisdiction of the Guangyuan area allows the ownership of this theatre to be inferred in turn.
cause: 打起來有遠因也有近因。遠因是南北對峙近百年而蜀道北段卡在兩國之間：利州是蜀道北門，誰據了它，誰就握有進取漢中與隴右的跳板，陳朝自建國以來一直想取利州打通北方通道，蜀地士人也有北上的心事；同時北周的益州、梁州與陳的劍門、昭化線幾十年犬牙交錯，邊將之間的衝突與馬匹糧食的往來糾紛，隨時可能升級成兵事。近因則是北周在580年集大軍南下的同時，陳朝判定北周主力已盡投豫東睢陽方向，蜀北防守必然空虛，遂從益州調兵北上，尋求在另一條戰線上換回一場勝利。這是一步險棋：陳朝國內主和與主戰之爭正酣，宣帝久病，宗室與文臣互相猜忌，邊將多有冒功之心，急著在主將拍板之前搶先下手；北周這邊的算盤同樣清楚，宇文護需要一場對外勝利來鞏固關隴集團的權位，楊堅則要在南征中累積兵功與威望。兩家的算盤都指向同一條邊界，衝突於是無法避免。
causeEn: There were distant causes and immediate ones. The distant cause was that the two states had faced one another for nearly a century while the northern stretch of the Shu road was lodged between them. Lizhou was the northern gate of the Shu road, and whoever held it held the springboard for an advance into Hanzhong and Longyou; ever since its foundation the Chen court had wanted to take Lizhou and open a road to the north, and the gentry of Shu had their own reasons for looking that way. At the same time the Zhou prefectures of Yizhou and Liangzhou and the Chen line of Jianmen and Zhaohua had been interleaved for decades, and quarrels between frontier commanders, together with disputes over horses and grain, could at any moment swell into fighting. The immediate cause was this: while the Zhou was concentrating its great army for the southern campaign in 580, the Chen court judged that the Zhou main force had been thrown entirely into the Suiyang direction in eastern Henan and that the defence of the northern Shu road must stand empty, and so it moved troops north out of Yizhou to try to win a battle on a different front in exchange. It was a dangerous gamble. Debate in the Chen court between advocates of peace and advocates of war was at its height, the Xuan emperor had been ill for a long while, the imperial clan and the civil officials were suspicious of one another, and frontier commanders with a taste for false credit were eager to strike before the capital had settled the matter. The Zhou calculation was just as clear: Yuwen Hu needed a victory abroad to confirm the position of the Guanzhong group, while Yang Jian meant to pile up military credit and prestige in the southern campaign. Both courts were aiming at the same boundary line, and the clash was bound to happen.
impact: 就眼前看，利州沒有易手，蜀道北門仍在陳軍手中，但陳軍的攻勢止步於劍門以北，兩家在蜀北的拉鋸從此轉為長期的邊境消耗。陳朝把兵力和糧秣分散在南北兩條戰線上，益州各郡久役疲敝，國內怨言漸熾；同年豫東與蜀北兩處都沒有換來捷報，這份空虛在陳宣帝於582年病逝後被宗室與後主之間的權力爭鬥放大，成為陳朝末年崩解的伏線。北方這一邊，隋篡周之後，蜀北防務由韋世康、韋沖等相繼出掌益州總管者整頓，城壘修葺、徭役加派、驛傳恢復，蜀地士人對新政的怨望同時累積，589年隋軍南下時蜀中人心已不附陳。技術層面上，這場交鋒也留下清楚教訓：蜀道地勢與守方弩砲、連發弩的組合，使任何仰攻劍門以北城池的嘗試都要付出極高代價，此後歷代攻蜀必先取劍門、斷其糧道而不強攻利州，先斷蜀道遂成為西南用兵的固定邏輯。卡面秦連弩所代表的弩機儲力技術，在六世紀的攻城戰中依然是守方抵禦密集步兵的主要手段。
impactEn: In the short run Lizhou did not change hands and the northern gate of the Shu road stayed in the hands of the Chen, but the Chen advance halted north of Jianmen, and from that point the tug of war in the north of Shu became a long contest of attrition on the frontier. The Chen state had spread its soldiers and provisions over two fronts, north and south; the commanderies of Yizhou were worn out by long service and resentment at home grew. Since neither the eastern front in the Henan nor the northern front in Shu brought a victory in the same year, the emptiness of that year was enlarged after the Xuan emperor died in 582 by the struggle for power between the imperial clan and the last emperor, and it became one of the threads that later unravelled the whole Chen state. On the northern side, once the Sui had replaced the Zhou, the defence of the northern Shu road was reorganised by the men who in turn held the inspector-generalship of Yizhou, among them Wei Shikang and Wei Chong: walls were repaired, corvée was increased and the post roads restored, while the resentment of the Shu gentry against the new administration piled up at the same time, so that by 589, when the Sui army came south, the people of Shu were no longer attached to the Chen. At the level of technique the campaign also left a clear lesson. The combination of the Shu terrain with the bolt shooters and repeating crossbows of the defenders made any attempt to storm a city north of Jianmen pay an extremely high price; from then on every power that attacked Shu first took Jianmen and cut its supply road rather than assaulting Lizhou directly, and the principle of cutting the Shu road first became fixed logic in southwestern warfare. The stored-power crossbow mechanism represented by the Qin repeating crossbow on this card remained in the sixth century the chief means by which a defender held off dense infantry.
result: 陳軍沒有打下利州，攻城器械與士氣都在蜀道上耗盡，終究退回劍門一線；利州與蜀道北段仍由北周方面控制，陳朝蜀境的第一道防線維持在劍門、昭化。守方保住城邑卻也消耗了守軍與糧秣，蜀道沿線的堡壘與烽燧自此更加緊密。580年留下的這條線，在兩條戰線同時拉鋸的消耗下成為僵局：雙方都沒有餘力再發動新的大役，而僵局對正在集兵備船的北方更為有利。從更長的視角看，這是隋文帝楊堅十年之後滅陳的結構性前提之一：陳朝在蜀北與豫東兩處都被擋住，兩個方向都被拉成消耗戰，邊界線沒有移動，國力卻一年比一年薄。等到開皇八年隋軍大舉南下，陳朝已沒有第二支可以調動的兵團可用。關於此役的具體經過、雙方出兵數目與將佐姓名，現存史料只留寥寥數語，細節多有不可確證之處；本紀所敘以可判定的地理、編制、兵器與後果為主，未詳處不作臆補。
resultEn: The Chen army did not take Lizhou. Its siege equipment and its morale were both spent on the Shu road, and in the end it fell back to the line of Jianmen. Lizhou and the northern stretch of the Shu road remained under Zhou control, and the first line of defence of the Chen borderlands stayed at Jianmen and Zhaohua. The defenders saved their city but at the cost of their garrison and their provisions, and the forts and beacon towers along the road were thereafter made more closely spaced. The line left standing in 580 became a deadlock under the attrition of two fronts fought at once: neither side had the strength to launch another great campaign, and the deadlock suited the north, which was meanwhile gathering troops and building ships. Seen from the longer perspective, this was one of the structural preconditions for Yang Jian, the Sui emperor, to destroy Chen ten years later. The Chen state was held off in the north of Shu and in eastern Henan alike, both directions were converted into a war of attrition, the boundary line did not move, and yet the strength of the state thinned year by year. By the eighth year of Kaihuang, when the Sui army came south in force, the Chen had no second army corps left to move. As for the course of the battle itself, the numbers of troops on each side and the names of the commanders, the surviving sources leave only a few words, and many details cannot be confirmed; this account therefore sets out what can be determined from the geography, the order of battle, the arms and the consequences, and makes no conjecture where the record is silent.
